items: Export all open tabs to a bookmark folder named with today's date before you start clearing, so nothing is lost during the cleanup process and the fear of losing information doesn't stop you.
Install a tab counter extension to determine your exact tab count, since most people discover they have ten times more tabs than they originally estimated.

Open 10 random tabs from your bookmark archive and categorize each one by asking whether it is current research, a reference you will use this week, a forgotten saved item, or a duplicate of another tab.
Write down your total tab count so you can measure progress and stay motivated throughout the entire cleanup process, which typically takes several weeks.
Set a 25-minute timer for each tab-clearing session and commit to stopping completely when the timer ends, regardless of how many tabs remain unprocessed.
Open only 10 tabs from your archive at a time and make a definitive decision on each one by choosing to read it now, bookmark it properly in a specific folder, or close it immediately.
Create specific bookmark folders for each topic rather than using generic labels like miscellaneous or read later, because specific organization makes tabs easier to locate later.
Close any tab you cannot honestly commit to reading within the next 7 days, since saved-but-forgotten tabs are exactly what created this problem in the first place.
Set a personal rule to never end the day with more than 20 open tabs and enforce this limit by closing existing tabs before opening any new ones.
Apply the one-in-one-out rule by closing an existing tab for every new tab you open, which keeps your total tab count stable without feeling overly restrictive.
Perform a 10-minute weekly review every Friday afternoon to close tabs you have not touched in 7 days, consolidate duplicate tabs, and move research tabs into bookmark folders.
Track your daily tab count until it consistently stays below 50, which typically takes about three weeks of consistent practice to establish as a permanent habit.
